The quantity of electricity on a planetary ellipsoid maintained
at potential $V$ in an infinite field, is
$$Q=c \frac{V}{\frac{1}{2} \pi-\gamma},$$
(37)
where $c \sec \gamma$ is the equatorial, radius, and $c \tan \gamma$ is the polar
radius.
If $\gamma=0$, the figure is a circular disk of radius $c$, and
$$\begin{aligned}
\sigma & =\frac{V}{2 \pi^{2} \sqrt{c^{2}-r^{2}}} \\
Q & =c \frac{V}{\frac{1}{2} \pi}
\end{aligned}$$
(38)

152.] Second Case. Let $b=c$, then $k=1$ and $k^{\prime}=0$,
$$a=\log \tan \frac{\pi+2 \theta}{4}, \text { whence } \lambda_{1}=c \tanh a,$$
(40)
and the equation of the hyperboloids of revolution of two sheets
becomes
$$\frac{x^{2}}{(\tanh a)^{2}}-\frac{y^{2}+z^{2}}{(\operatorname{sech} a)^{2}}=c^{2} .$$
(41)
The quantity $\beta$ becomes reduced to $\phi$, and each of the hyper-
boloids of one sheet is reduced to a pair of planes intersecting
in the axis of $x$ whose equation is
$$\frac{y^{2}}{(\sin \beta)^{2}}-\frac{z^{2}}{(\cos \beta)^{2}}=0$$
(42)
This is a system of meridional planes in which $\beta$ is the longitude.
The quantity $\gamma$ as defined in page 233, (7), becomes in this case
infinite at the lower limit. To avoid this let us define it as the
value of the integral
$$\int_{\lambda_{2}}^{\infty} \frac{c d \lambda_{3}}{\lambda_{3}^{2}-c^{2}}$$
If we then put $\lambda_{3}=c \sec \psi$, we find $\gamma=\int_{\psi}^{\frac{\pi}{2} d \psi} \sin \psi$, whence
$\lambda_{3}=c \operatorname{coth} \gamma$, and the equation of the family of ellipsoids is
$$\frac{x^{2}}{(\operatorname{coth} \gamma)^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}+z^{2}}{(\operatorname{cosech} \gamma)^{2}}=c^{2} .$$
(43)
These ellipsoids, in which the transverse axis is the axis of
revolution, are called ovary ellipsoids.
The quantity of electricity on an ovary ellipsoid maintained
at potential $V$ in an infinite field becomes in this case, by (29),
$$c V \div \int_{\psi_{0}}^{\frac{\pi}{8}} \frac{d \psi}{\sin \psi}$$
(44)
where $c \sec \psi_{0}$ is the polar radius.
